title: Good to Great
author: Jim Collins
one_line_takeaway: Companies go from good to great not through a single bold stroke but through disciplined people, disciplined thought and disciplined action compounding over years, led by humble but relentless leaders.
synopsis: Jim Collins and a team of researchers screened 1,435 Fortune 500 companies for the rare ones whose stock returns were at or below the market for fifteen years, hit a transition point, and then beat the market by at least three times over the next fifteen. Eleven qualified — among them Abbott, Circuit City, Fannie Mae, Gillette, Kimberly-Clark, Kroger, Nucor, Philip Morris, Pitney Bowes, Walgreens and Wells Fargo — and each was paired with a comparison company in the same industry that had the same opportunities but didn't make the leap. What separated them was not strategy documents, pay, technology or mergers, but a consistent pattern: Level 5 leaders who combine personal humility with fierce professional will; getting the right people on the bus before deciding where to drive it; confronting brutal facts while keeping faith in the outcome (the Stockdale Paradox); a simple Hedgehog Concept at the intersection of what a company can be best in the world at, what drives its economic engine and what its people are passionate about; a culture of discipline rather than a tyrant who imposes it; technology used as an accelerator rather than a cause; and steady pushing of a flywheel instead of the lurching restructurings of the doom loop. Collins closes by tying these findings to the enduring companies of his earlier book, Built to Last.

chapters.title: Good Is the Enemy of Great
chapters.core_claim: Most companies never become great precisely because being good is comfortable, and a rigorous comparison of the few that made the leap shows greatness follows from identifiable, learnable principles.
key_points: Good is the enemy of great: settling for good is the main reason so few organizations become great.

The research screened 1,435 Fortune 500 companies and found eleven whose cumulative returns went from at or below the market to at least three times the market for fifteen years after a transition point.

Each good-to-great company was matched with a direct comparison company in the same industry with similar opportunities that failed to make the leap, plus unsustained comparisons that jumped and fell back.
The eleven companies' post-transition returns averaged about 6.9 times the general market over fifteen years.
The findings form a framework of disciplined people, disciplined thought and disciplined action, driven by a flywheel of buildup and breakthrough.
Collins insisted the team let the evidence speak rather than start from a theory, which is how unexpected findings such as Level 5 leadership emerged.

chapters.title: Level 5 Leadership
chapters.core_claim: Every good-to-great transition was led by a Level 5 leader who channels ambition into the company rather than into personal glory, blending humility with an unwavering will to do what must be done.
key_points: Level 5 sits atop a hierarchy: highly capable individual, contributing team member, competent manager, effective leader, and the Level 5 executive who builds enduring greatness through humility plus will.
Darwin Smith at Kimberly-Clark sold the company's traditional paper mills and bet it on consumer products like Kleenex and Huggies, going head to head with Procter & Gamble.
Level 5 leaders look out the window to credit others when things go well and in the mirror to take responsibility when they go badly.
They set up successors to succeed, whereas many comparison companies had charismatic, larger-than-life leaders whose companies faltered after they left.
Most good-to-great CEOs came from inside the company; celebrity outsiders brought in as saviors correlated negatively with sustained transformation.
Collins told his team to downplay the role of top executives, but the data kept pointing back to this distinctive leadership pattern.

chapters.title: First Who . . . Then What
chapters.core_claim: Good-to-great leaders first got the right people on the bus, the wrong people off it and the right people in the right seats, and only then decided where to drive it.
key_points: Starting with 'who' rather than 'what' makes a company adaptable: the right people will find the right direction and don't need to be managed or motivated into it.
Comparison companies often followed a 'genius with a thousand helpers' model, which collapsed when the genius left.
Wells Fargo under Dick Cooley and Carl Reichardt hired outstanding people ahead of banking deregulation, without knowing exactly what they'd do.
Be rigorous, not ruthless: when in doubt, don't hire and keep looking; when a people change is needed, act; put your best people on your biggest opportunities, not your biggest problems.
Executive compensation showed no systematic link to the transitions; pay attracts and keeps the right people rather than motivating the wrong ones.

chapters.title: Confront the Brutal Facts (Yet Never Lose Faith)
chapters.core_claim: Great decisions flow from honestly confronting reality, which requires a climate where the truth is heard, combined with unwavering faith that the company will prevail in the end.
key_points: Kroger faced the evidence that the old grocery model was dying and rebuilt its whole system around superstores, while A&P ignored what its own experiments told it and declined.

Leaders create a climate where the truth is heard by leading with questions rather than answers, engaging in dialogue and debate rather than coercion, conducting autopsies without blame, and building red-flag mechanisms.
A charismatic leader can become a liability when people filter bad news to avoid displeasing them.
The Stockdale Paradox, named for Admiral Jim Stockdale's survival as a POW in Vietnam: keep faith that you will prevail while confronting the most brutal facts of your current reality.
Stockdale observed that the optimists who expected release by Christmas were the prisoners who didn't make it out.

chapters.title: The Hedgehog Concept (Simplicity within the Three Circles)
chapters.core_claim: Good-to-great companies built a simple, crystal-clear concept from the intersection of three circles and then pursued it with fanatical consistency.
key_points: Drawing on Isaiah Berlin's essay 'The Hedgehog and the Fox', Collins argues the great companies were hedgehogs who reduced a complex world to one organizing idea.
The three circles are what you can be the best in the world at (and what you cannot), what drives your economic engine, and what you are deeply passionate about.
The economic engine is captured by a single 'profit per X' denominator, such as Walgreens' profit per customer visit or Wells Fargo's profit per employee.
A Hedgehog Concept is an understanding of what you can be best at, not a goal or a plan to be best, and being merely good at your core business is not enough.
Reaching it took about four years on average, through an iterative process; Collins describes a 'Council' of key people who repeatedly debate the questions.
Walgreens committed to convenient drugstores and outperformed Eckerd, which chased unrelated diversification.

chapters.title: A Culture of Discipline
chapters.core_claim: Sustained results come from a culture of self-disciplined people who take disciplined action within a framework of freedom and responsibility, not from a tyrant imposing discipline.
key_points: Hire self-disciplined people who don't need to be managed, then manage the system rather than the people.
Comparison companies often had tyrannical disciplinarians who got short-term results that faded after they left, such as Stanley Gault at Rubbermaid.
Discipline means adhering fanatically to the Hedgehog Concept and saying no to opportunities outside the three circles, however attractive.
Collins recommends a 'stop doing' list and redirecting resources away from anything that doesn't fit.
Triathlete Dave Scott rinsing his cottage cheese to remove extra fat illustrates the kind of rigor great companies show.

chapters.title: Technology Accelerators
chapters.core_claim: Technology accelerates momentum a company already has but never creates it; great companies apply carefully selected technologies that fit their Hedgehog Concept.
key_points: Good-to-great companies became pioneers in the application of technologies directly linked to their three circles and ignored fads outside them.
In interviews, most good-to-great executives didn't rank technology among the top five factors in their transitions.
Walgreens took a 'crawl, walk, run' approach to the internet during the dot-com frenzy while a rival rushed in.
Nucor's mini-mill steelmaking shows technology applied in service of a clear concept.
Reacting to technological change out of fear is a sign of mediocrity.

chapters.title: The Flywheel and the Doom Loop
chapters.core_claim: Transformations that look dramatic from outside were cumulative processes inside — pushing a flywheel turn upon turn until breakthrough — while comparison companies lurched through the doom loop.
key_points: There was no single defining action, grand program or miracle moment; people inside often didn't realize a transformation was happening.
Consistent pushes in one direction build momentum until the flywheel breaks through, and visible results attract people and resources, feeding further momentum.
Comparison companies fell into the doom loop: launching new programs with fanfare, reacting to events, changing direction and restructuring repeatedly.
Big acquisitions did not produce breakthroughs; good-to-great companies made acquisitions after the flywheel was turning, as accelerators.
Many good-to-great companies never gave their transformation a name or a slogan.

chapters.title: From Good to Great to Built to Last
chapters.core_claim: The good-to-great principles are the prequel to Built to Last: they turn a good organization into a great one, and preserving core values while stimulating progress keeps it great.
key_points: The concepts from Built to Last — core values and a purpose beyond making money, preserving the core while stimulating progress — sustain greatness once it is reached.
Big Hairy Audacious Goals work best when set within the Hedgehog Concept rather than out of bravado.
Enduring companies need a purpose beyond profit, but the good-to-great findings are what build the momentum in the first place.
Collins argues becoming great is no harder than staying good, and that meaningful work is its own reason to pursue greatness.
